draft.title: Historians' interpretations
card: An interpretation is a historian's explanation of what happened and why. Different historians can interpret the same events differently.
Evidence
Historians may use different sources, or give more weight to some sources than to others.
Questions
Historians ask different questions. One may study leaders and battles, while another studies the lives of ordinary people.
Time
The time a historian writes in shapes the view too. New evidence can appear, and the values and concerns of the day change.
draft.remember: Evidence, questions and the time of writing all shape an interpretation.

a.q: Two historians study the same event and reach different conclusions. Which is a likely reason?
opts: They asked different questions about the event
They used a different calendar to date the event
One of them was not allowed to use any sources
The event happened differently for each of them
a.why: Different questions lead historians to look at different evidence and reach different conclusions. The event itself happened only one way, so the difference lies in how it is studied.
a.clue: Think about what each historian set out to find out.

b.q: In 1950 a historian wrote about a colonial town using only official reports. In 2015 another used diaries and oral histories of local residents as well, and reached a different view. What best explains the difference?
opts: The evidence used and the time of writing differed
The first historian made up the official reports
Only the later historian can ever be correct
The town changed after the first book was written
b.why: The two historians used different evidence and wrote in different times, with different concerns. The later view is not automatically correct, because it is also an interpretation. Neither case suggests the reports were invented.
b.clue: Compare the sources each historian used and when each wrote.

a.best: They asked different questions about the event

b.best: The evidence used and the time of writing differed

problems.detail: The clue ('Compare the sources each historian used and when each wrote') names both parts of the right option, evidence and time of writing, so a student can match it without knowing the idea.
